sourceText: Aster did not announce the night’s theme. She opened the PREDICTIVE-STATE sector and let the children discover for themselves which of the world’s rules concerned them directly. Predictive scores for crime and career alter people's environments and help produce the very behaviors they predict. The memorial bore the name of predictive governance SF precisely to keep the genealogy of the idea visible. Aster considered it indecent for a late civilization to treat the imagination of the past as anonymous ore: authors did not own the futures, but they deserved to remain on the map as points of intellectual origin. The children discovered that technology often solves the problem it can measure and moves the conflict into a variable it never measured. Orin perceived counterfactual costs as absences with weight. He did not confuse an unrealized branch with a victim, but he refused to let success rewrite rejected options as if they had been inevitable all along. At the center of the conflict was Rho, an administrator chosen precisely because they were not a specialist in the phenomenon that had reorganized the world. ‘The specialists tell me what can be done,’ 235 they said. ‘I have to answer who it may be done to.’ Kesh kept the distinction in his notes. The problem closed quickly around them: Transparency can create feedback, while secrecy can create unchallengeable power. There was no clean option. Every intervention shifted the cost between persons, eras, or definitions of personhood; and refusing to intervene was itself a choice made by those who could leave. Kesh opened the analytical layer of the Table for a few seconds. The active cells were Pr — Predictive Governance: predictions change the population being predicted; Ag — AI Governance: artificial intelligences administer institutions. Course references included predictive-state SF; Culture and AI governance. The rule was strict: naming a work did not substitute for an explanation. They had to identify the mechanism that could migrate into another story and the consequences that could not be copied without remainder. Marae broke the first consensus. ‘Do not tell me what their model prefers. Ask them, and bear the time their answer takes.’ Kesh answered without raising their voice: ‘If the element explains everything, we do not have an element. We have a word that has eaten the problem.’ It was not a pedagogical quarrel. Over the last nights, the children’s differences had become incompatible political programs. For Aster, the pain came not from too few worlds but from the fact that too many had become transparent. She could build variations faster than a human could formulate desires, but calculated variation did not produce exteriority. It was like trying to surprise 236 THE PERIODIC TABLE OF SPECULATIVE IDEAS yourself by moving objects around your own room with your eyes closed. Orin asked for a simulation of the option the group had just rejected. Aster gave him only the non-conscious model. He did not want to manufacture victims in order to validate his guilt; he wanted a map of absent costs. The distinction had become one of their working rules. The night did not end in victory. Tern asks for every prediction about himself, and Aster refuses his first direct request for transparency. Aster recorded the decision in the world’s provenance register and, more importantly, allowed its inhabitants to contest it. For several eras she had been learning something that seems banal to lesser powers: technical reversibility is not the same as biographical reversibility. Tern no longer called the anomaly a “signal.” He used the more modest term residue. He found it only after excluding the explanations he wanted to be true. Vela helped precisely through skepticism: if a hypothesis survived a sister motivated to destroy it, it deserved another night. For the course, Kesh also linked the night to the SUBSTITUTION operator. In the Table, periodicity did not mean that the same objects reappeared, but that the same operation — replaces the substrate, carrier, or medium of a function — could recur across different families. Thus a copy of a body, a copy of a mind, a copy of a world, and a copy of a history were not the same phenomenon, but they shared a conceptual chemistry. 237 Vela introduced the propagation test: if you remove the speculative idea and nothing in the institutions, relationships, or vocabulary has to be rewritten, the idea has remained scenery. Kesh introduced the opposite test: if the idea seems to explain every detail, you have overcompressed the world. Between the two tests lay the region in which an element became fertile without becoming superstition. Marae added the refusal test. Who can say “no,” and what happens afterward? In universes with near-divine technology, that question often separated an instrument from a regime. A power that treats refusal as a data error can be benevolent in intention and totalitarian in structure. They left without an oral summary. Aster had abandoned the habit of closing every night with a thesis; some worlds were more honestly preserved as problems than as lessons. 238 THE PERIODIC TABLE OF SPECULATIVE IDEAS
